Holder authorization working assumption, pending user preference: use a
revocable server-issued 256-bit opaque device credential together with the
authenticated Gateway user session. Store only its SHA-256 digest and scope it
to an active registration, exact user and organization, with bounded expiry.
Theft of both bearer credentials permits signing until revocation; no
device-held asymmetric private key is introduced. The first local Rust
foundation is `marty-device-registration::holder_credential`: it returns the
bearer only at issuance, denies any registration carrying the old PS256 public-key
projection, and rejects wrong token, user, organization, registration,
expiry, revocation and inactivity. Its library suite passes 4/4 and
warnings-denied Clippy passes. This module is **not wired to an HTTP route or
persistent repository**, and does not create, authorize or sign with a durable
KMS holder key. Complete transactional credential rotation/revocation,
reference-only key persistence, authenticated Device Registration-to-Signing
Keys operations, Gateway session binding and mobile/web wallet behavior
before calling this accepted custody.

2026-10-09 local holder-credential durability follow-up: the Rust Device
Registration fresh schema now has a digest-only `device_holder_credentials`
table scoped to registration, user and organization, with a single-current
index, bounded lifetime and revocation constraints. A repository rotates the
current digest in one PostgreSQL transaction under the registration row lock;
explicit revocation and device deactivation revoke it. The credential lookup
returns only digest and scope metadata. A disposable PostgreSQL integration
test passed issuance storage, authorization, rotation, wrong-scope rejection,
transaction rollback on duplicate ID, explicit revocation and deactivation
revocation. This is local, unpushed evidence. It does not establish an
authenticated enrollment route, a durable KMS holder key, holder signing or
wallet acceptance; those remain release blockers.

2026-10-09 holder enrollment security review: the current native Device
Registration `register` path accepts a keyless registration under an
authenticated Gateway session with no device challenge; the challenge is
required only when a PS256 public key is supplied. Therefore the proposed
session plus server-issued bearer is revocable and KMS-compatible, but its
initial enrollment does not independently prove control of a particular
device. A stolen Gateway session could register and receive a fresh bearer.
Do not expose holder signing on that basis alone. The cutover needs an
explicit enrollment and rotation authorization decision (for example,
step-up user authentication or an independent device pairing ceremony),
while keeping the actual holder signing key generated and retained in KMS.
Signing Keys currently offers only public-JWK `holder-keys` registration,
and the VC-API holder-proof path creates and deletes a one-request OpenBao
key. Neither is a durable holder signer. The next implementation must pair
a registration-scoped, reference/public-only key ledger with authenticated
Device Registration-to-Signing Keys create/sign/revoke operations and must
reject arbitrary provider references at that boundary. The published UI run
`37929521793` is still live: 19 of 21 jobs completed without a failure;
OpenBao integration-secret recovery and Canvas public image build are active.

2026-10-09 local durable holder-key reference work: native Device Registration
now has a fresh-schema `device_holder_keys` ledger containing only a
registration/user/organization/purpose, OpenBao reference and version, and
public Ed25519 or P-256 coordinates. It contains no JWK blob or private key
column. The Rust projection accepts only active non-exportable provider
metadata, validates the public coordinates and binds the reference to the
organization hash. PostgreSQL binding locks the registration, rotates the
current purpose entry atomically and revokes entries on deactivation. The
Device Registration library and integration suite passed 16/16, including
fresh PostgreSQL migration, reference rotation and rollback. Synthetic
provider metadata in these tests proves storage behavior only, not live KMS
custody. OpenBao's [Transit sign API](https://openbao.org/docs/next/api/secret/transit/)
documents `key_version`; the local Signing Keys adapter now selects the
matching public-key version, sends a positive explicit version for signing
and rejects a response tagged with another version. Its focused regression
test passes. The ledger and adapter are local, unpushed, and not connected to
an enrollment/signing route. Provisioning compensation, remote revoke,
dedicated service authentication, a live versioned OpenBao signature, and
wallet behavior remain required. UI CI `37929521793` remains live with
20/21 jobs complete and no failure; Canvas is still active.

Holder namespace/policy review: the first local ledger draft used
`holder-*`, which the shipped signing-keys-managed OpenBao policy cannot

Only those two namespaces now permit deletion after an explicit

2026-10-09 local managed holder service boundary: a shared Rust reference

for holder and presenter keys; the fresh Device Registration schema enforces

credential, rather than the broad internal signing credential. The provider

2026-10-09 local remote holder-deletion follow-up: fresh Device Registration
schema now includes a reference-only deletion queue. Replacing a holder key or
deactivating a device commits local revocation and queue insertion in the same
PostgreSQL transaction; a failed replacement rolls both back. A Rust worker
uses the dedicated Device Registration-to-Signing Keys credential, retries
failed revocations after a bounded delay, and marks completion only after the
remote service confirms key absence. The Signing Keys revoke operation is
idempotent after OpenBao deletion and verifies absence through the managed
key lookup and scoped inventory before reporting success. A fresh disposable
PostgreSQL plus HTTP test passed rollback, deactivation, failed-call retry and
completion behavior; the disposable OpenBao probe passed repeated revocation.
The worker is enabled only with its paired origin and credential, which are
not yet provisioned in supported deployment profiles. Remote creation and
signing are also not yet called by Device Registration, and provisioning
compensation remains open. The HTTP retry test proves scheduling behavior;
the separate OpenBao probe proves actual remote deletion. Neither is an
end-to-end wallet acceptance test.

2026-10-09 local holder creation compensation: Device Registration and Signing
Keys now share the strict Rust holder-key request/scope contract. Device
Registration has one dedicated client for create/sign/revoke, reused by its
cleanup worker. Before a remote create, the repository reserves the scoped
reference in a fresh-schema provision ledger. Binding public KMS metadata
requires that live reservation in the same transaction that retires the old
key; an expired, failed or interrupted unbound reservation is eligible for
the remote cleanup worker. The internal provisioner checks the exact user,
organization and active keyless registration, reserves, calls Signing Keys,
validates non-exportable public metadata and binds it; on an ordinary error it
accelerates cleanup, while a process crash still leaves the original durable
deadline. Fresh PostgreSQL tests passed reservation-required binding,
rollback, stale-provision cleanup and a disposable dedicated-client create
call. This client and provisioner have no public enrollment route yet. The
test create service returns synthetic metadata, so live combined Device
Registration-to-Signing Keys-to-OpenBao behavior still needs acceptance.
The Device Registration client and binding projection also reject private
material anywhere in returned metadata, rather than checking only the
projected public JWK.

2026-10-09 local internal signing authorization: Rust Device Registration now

2026-10-09 local clock-safe bearer issuance: the PostgreSQL credential

atomically revokes the old digest and stores the new digest before returning

issuance route; its caller authorization policy remains a release gate.

2026-10-09 applicant liveness architecture audit: the native applicant
service currently has no Signing Keys client, challenge route, or persisted
single-use challenge state. Its biometric enrollment accepts raw capture data
but cannot establish liveness. The Signing Keys `/internal/kms/sign` endpoint
accepts arbitrary caller-supplied provider configuration and payload behind a
shared internal API key, so it is too broad to expose to a mobile client or
use directly as a purpose-bound liveness authority. A production design needs
a dedicated server-side challenge issuer with a configured non-exportable KMS
key, a canonical signed payload binding challenge ID, nonce, authenticated
applicant/organization, gestures, issued/expiry times and purpose, plus
durable atomic consume-once state. Submission must authenticate the caller,
verify the KMS signature and challenge binding, reject expiry/replay and
validate actual device capture evidence before setting a verified result.
Do not treat the present UI mock capture or client-supplied biometric template
as that evidence. This audit narrows the next implementation contract; no
production liveness claim is made.

2026-10-09 mobile liveness ownership correction: the Authenticator's

camera frames or a capture evidence artifact, and has no production
authentication/submission handlers. No source path connects this flow to the
native applicant service. Therefore adding an applicant challenge endpoint
alone would not satisfy the mobile requirement, and KMS signing a challenge
would establish challenge origin but not physical liveness. First establish
the actual product submission owner and server-verifiable capture-evidence
contract, then wire a purpose-bound KMS issuer and atomic replay state at that
owner. Keep the current production mobile path fail closed in the meantime.

K6 Azure HSM self-review found a concrete public-key interoperability gap.
[Azure's Get Key contract](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/rest/api/keyvault/keys/get-key/get-key?view=rest-keyvault-keys-2025-07-01)
returns `EC-HSM` or `RSA-HSM` as `kty` for HSM-backed keys, while issuer
selection and certificate checks require standard public JWK `EC`/`RSA`.
The local Signing Keys adapter now normalizes those two Azure public types
before projecting the JWK and strips private members as before. The focused
test passed, the full Signing Keys library suite passed 143 tests with eight
expected opt-in ignores, Rustfmt passed, and warnings-denied library Clippy
passed under Rust 1.95 on Windows. This change is local and should be batched
with other K6 corrections into one UI PR push; a live Azure HSM enrollment,
sign and certificate flow is still required before claiming provider support.
The provider-neutral HTTP golden vector now supplies an Azure `EC-HSM` Get
Key response and expects a public `EC` JWK; its full public-key-discovery
test passed, covering the request, response and private-member stripping.

K6 AWS signing self-review found a payload-size and algorithm-binding gap.
[AWS KMS Sign](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/APIReference/API_Sign.html)
limits RAW messages to 4096 bytes and documents DIGEST mode for larger
pre-hashed input. The local adapter now hashes the supported JOSE RSA/ECDSA
payload once, sends `MessageType=DIGEST`, maps the JOSE algorithm to the
matching AWS signing algorithm in one Rust function shared with public-key
discovery, and rejects conflicting native overrides before network I/O.
The provider HTTP golden vector now expects the digest request; its signing
test passed. A mismatched-algorithm negative and an 8-KiB digest boundary
test passed. The complete Signing Keys library suite passed 144 tests with
eight expected opt-in ignores; warnings-denied library Clippy and Rustfmt
passed. This is local and should join the Azure correction in one UI push.
Real AWS KMS enrollment, long-input signing and certificate binding still
need credentials and live acceptance before K6 can close.

K6 cloud-auth scope remains larger than the two crypto fixes. The service
catalog advertises AWS `iam_role`/`access_key`/`assume_role`, Azure
`managed_identity`/`client_secret`/`certificate`, and GCP
`workload_identity`/`service_account`. Current AWS signing uses the SDK
default credential chain regardless of the registered `auth_mode` and
`auth_reference`; Azure/GCP request builders only attach `auth_reference`
as a literal bearer token and do not acquire an identity token. The
validation policy can report managed/workload identity modes as selected
before those adapters actually authenticate. This is a real supported-path
gap, not a reason to remove the advertised modes. Implement provider-native
credential resolution and tenant-scoped reference handling in Rust, then
exercise the selected auth modes and sign/public-key/certificate flows with
live provider identities. Until then, K6 and cloud-provider release claims
remain open even if HTTP stubs and OpenBao live tests pass.

2026-10-10 K6 credential-custody finding: the signing registry serializes its
normalized service document directly into tenant-keyed Redis, including the
`auth_reference` field (`registry.rs` `save_with_rotation_lease` and
`normalize_service`). The public GET masks the field, but masking does not
protect the stored value. Today OpenBao token mode uses the field as a literal
token; Azure/GCP also use it as a literal bearer token, while AWS ignores it.
Calling it a “reference” in the wizard therefore overstates the storage and
provider contracts. Do not route cloud credentials through this field as
plaintext or silently fall through to the process-wide AWS identity. The
canonical Rust solution must define a tenant- and service-bound credential
reference, store any required credential bytes under the dedicated
non-exportable integration-secret Transit envelope (or use provider-native
workload identity without stored bytes), resolve only for the matching
provider/auth mode at operation time, and preserve the current public masking
and unchanged-connection update semantics. Remove plaintext credential storage
at the cutover; no compatibility migration is needed because there are no
public deployments. Test cross-tenant/service rebinding rejection, changed
endpoint/auth-mode clearing, KMS outage fail-closed behavior, and each provider
mode before making a cloud BYOK release claim. The existing OpenBao
registration-to-issuer live evidence does not qualify cloud credential custody.
Provider-mode implementation must honor the KMS-only private-key boundary:
AWS `assume_role` can use scoped STS credentials, Azure `certificate` must
use a remotely held/non-exportable signing key for the client assertion, and
GCP `service_account` must mean workload identity or service-account
impersonation, never an imported service-account JSON private key. This is a
contract clarification for the catalog, not authorization to drop those
onboarding capabilities. AWS SDK for Rust documents that its unpinned default
chain may select process environment keys, shared files, web identity, or
container credentials; selecting `iam_role` in the UI does not currently
force role credentials. Sources: [AWS credential providers](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sdk-for-rust/latest/dg/credproviders.html),
[AWS AssumeRole Rust example](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sdk-for-rust/latest/dg/rust_sts_code_examples.html),
[GCP workload identity federation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/workload-identity-federation),
[GCP ADC credential risks](https://docs.cloud.google.com/docs/authentication/application-default-credentials),
[Azure Key Vault authentication](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/key-vault/general/developers-guide).

credential-envelope and redacted-config round-trip tests, all-target

unreleased cutover; existing plaintext rows fail closed and must be cleared.

2026-10-10 K6 AWS auth selection, local UI batch: the Rust AWS adapter now

2026-10-10 K6 Azure auth selection, local UI batch: the Rust Azure adapter now

2026-10-10 K8 response-bound self-review, held locally while the published
`e131e16fb` run executes: the shared Rust OpenBao envelope client still used
unbounded `reqwest::Response::json()` for Transit and HAIP responses. A
malformed or compromised backend could therefore force an excessive process
allocation before the operation failed. The local correction streams each
response into a bounded 4 MiB buffer and rejects malformed or oversized
JSON through one shared helper; redirects remain disabled. A focused
oversized-response test passed, the full non-opt-in Signing Keys package
suite passed (165 library tests, nine expected opt-in ignores), and
all-target warnings-denied Clippy passed. This local code requires its own
exact-head hosted qualification after batching with any findings from the
running CI; it is not evidence of live backend custody by itself.

CodeQL PR alert review on `be8fb4198` is recorded in the GitHub alert audit:
[#164](https://github.com/ElevenID/marty-ui/security/code-scanning/164)
is an intentional Azure managed-identity HTTP exception, dismissed as
`won't fix`. Microsoft's [VM IMDS token documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/managed-identities-azure-resources/how-to-use-vm-token)
specifies the link-local HTTP endpoint; [App Service documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/app-service/overview-managed-identity)
specifies a local `IDENTITY_ENDPOINT` and `X-IDENTITY-HEADER`. The implementation
restricts the endpoint to those local/link-local hosts, disables proxies and
redirects, and does not send an Azure client secret on this path. External
Azure OAuth and KMS destinations require HTTPS. Alerts
[#161](https://github.com/ElevenID/marty-ui/security/code-scanning/161) and
[#166](https://github.com/ElevenID/marty-ui/security/code-scanning/166)
were dismissed as false positives: their reported sinks are
`reqwest::RequestBuilder::send`, which executes a network request rather than
writing a log; the Signing Keys module has no logging call on those paths,
transport errors are discarded for fixed diagnostics, and provider bodies are
bounded and sanitized. The PR CodeQL check changed to success after these
recorded classifications. Re-evaluate if a future HTTP-client version or
logging configuration changes those properties.

2026-10-10 issuer-signing authorization review: Gateway's
`/internal/signing-keys/issuer-dids/sign` and Signing Keys'
`/internal/compat/issuer-dids/sign` check the dedicated issuer-signing
credential, then take `organization_id` from the caller's query/body. Flow,
Issuance and the Canvas sync worker share that credential across tenants.
The managed-profile binding ensures a requested key belongs to the supplied
organization, but it cannot prove the calling workload is entitled to act for
that organization. Merely rotating or further separating this shared static
credential would leave an authorized compromised workload able to select
another active tenant. Release qualification needs an independent tenant-bound
authorization proof tied to the operation, or tenant-isolated workload
identities with corresponding signer policy; the signer must verify that proof
before remote signing. A regression must demonstrate that a valid workload
credential with a different tenant context cannot reach the KMS signer while
normal Flow and Issuance issuance still succeeds. This is an open design and
implementation item, not a claim that KMS custody itself has failed.

2026-10-10 tenant authorization implementation constraint: source review of
`gateway/src/runtime.rs::internal_signing_compatibility_handler` and
`signing-keys/src/http.rs::issuer_did_sign` confirms that both authorize a
shared issuer-signing credential and then trust the caller-selected
`organization_id`. Gateway overwrites the JSON body with the query value, but
does not derive that value from an authenticated tenant identity. Native Flow
and Issuance each send their request's organization ID through this path.
The existing profile/key ownership check protects a key from being used under
the *wrong stated* organization; it does not authorize the workload to state
that organization. The final gate must bind each signing operation to tenant
authority established before the call, carry that binding through Gateway,
and verify it in Signing Keys before calling the remote signer. A candidate
operation capability would include tenant, audience, operation/payload digest,
short expiry and replay protection, signed by an authority that derives tenant
from an authenticated request or tenant-scoped persisted job. A generic mint
endpoint accepting a caller-supplied tenant would recreate the flaw. Trace
both synchronous Issuance and asynchronous Flow/Canvas origins before choosing
the proof format; add adversarial cross-tenant tests at Gateway and the direct
Signing Keys listener, plus normal issuance/Flow tests. This is design
guidance, not an implemented tenant boundary.

The same head's Canvas job failed only
`selfhost_public_image_loader_isolated` after its database suite reached the
packaged self-host preflight. The child exited with an incomplete packager
operation and the parent correctly withheld cleanup. Source tracing shows
that preflight calls the *same* `resolved_selfhost_runtime::qualify` closed

Tenant-signing origin trace for the next security feature: Flow constructs a
`SigningRequest` from its resolved `SigningIdentity.organization_id` in
`request_object.rs`; Issuance's `HttpDidSigner` forwards the credential or
passport operation's organization ID as Gateway query input; the Canvas LTI
tool path passes its configured organization into the same signer. Those
paths have different upstream authority sources, so adding a tenant string
or second shared credential at the common HTTP client is insufficient.
Before coding the verifier, trace and bind Flow's persisted flow ownership,
Issuance's authenticated API/job owner, and Canvas's configured tenant to an
operation-specific proof. Signing Keys must validate that proof and payload
binding directly, including direct-listener calls that bypass Gateway.

Further tenant-origin evidence: Gateway's public route middleware resolves an
organization from path/resource ownership/query/body/session and calls its
membership authorization provider before forwarding. Flow gRPC's
`start_flow` loads a stored definition, checks the authenticated principal's
`flow-instance:start` permission for that definition's organization, then
creates the instance under that organization. These are promising authority
sources for an operation grant, but the existing internal issuer-signing
route does not carry either authorization result to Signing Keys. A grant
must be minted from those checked contexts (or verified directly against
their authoritative stores), bind the exact sign input, and remain valid for
the asynchronous job lifetime without a reusable cross-tenant bearer.

Issuer-sign authorization source audit (2026-10-10): the direct Signing Keys
`issuer_did_sign` handler checks only the shared dedicated `x-api-key` before
passing `IssuerDidSignRequest` to the signing service. Gateway's internal
compatibility handler checks the same dedicated key, then accepts its
`organization_id` from a query parameter and forwards the body. Flow's HTTP
provider sends `request.organization_id` in both query and body, and its
request-object path fills that field from `SigningIdentity`. Thus neither a
Gateway hop nor the distinct issuer-sign key proves to Signing Keys that a
caller may sign for the selected tenant. This confirms the K6 tenant-authority
gap at the direct signing boundary. The corrective feature must bind a
verified operation owner, tenant, and exact payload to each sign request, with
Signing Keys performing validation before invoking remote KMS. Do not treat
client-supplied tenant equality between query/body as authorization.
`IssuerDidSignRequest` is also constructed inside Signing Keys for managed CSR
and certificate assembly, so a required external proof must attach at the
HTTP authorization boundary (or an explicit authorized-operation wrapper),
not be conflated with the internal cryptographic request type. The signing
service already resolves a tenant-scoped active profile and remote key, but
that establishes key selection, not caller permission. Gateway currently
replaces the upstream `x-api-key` with its own issuer credential and does not
forward a checked tenant context; Flow and Issuance can also call the route
without Gateway. A verifier at Signing Keys therefore needs a canonical,
purpose-scoped grant format and issuer-specific authority sources rather than
trusting the transport hop or profile lookup.

Token-scope self-review: the minted `didcomm-issuance` policy permits only
versioned public metadata reads and envelope pack operations; the live probe
now also rejects current-key reads and rotation. Its OpenBao ACL uses `+`
wildcards for tenant, key name, and version, however, so it is a service-wide
capability rather than an independently tenant-scoped KMS token. Native Rust
checks the request organization against the configured versioned reference
before use, but that is application authorization and must not be described
as an OpenBao per-tenant ACL. Tenant-bound operation authority and deployment
token lifecycle remain open security-review gates for production acceptance.
In the disposable OpenBao 2.5.5 dev probe the minted token had about 32 days
remaining and was renewable, but the current Compose overlay has no renewal
agent. Native Rust re-reads the token file on every request, allowing an
atomic operator replacement, yet no automated rotation/reissue path has been
qualified. The probe now requires finite renewable lifetime and denies
current-key metadata reads and sender-key rotation in addition to the earlier
administrative negatives.

`canvas-startup-fresh-run.json` attestation also pins the Python startup
scripts, their source hashes and the frozen corpus; CI requires and uploads
that artifact. Python image-startup fixture tests and the oracle producer
inventory reference the same corpus. Replace the runtime Python capture,
current-input sidecar and attestation schema together with native behavior

OpenBao workload-token lifecycle review (2026-10-10):
`scripts/bootstrap-selfhost-vault.sh` and `docker/openbao-selfhost-init.sh`
create orphan service, Signing Keys and DIDComm Issuance tokens without an
explicit period or TTL. The latter validates an existing DIDComm token's
policy and rejects an unusable one, while
`scripts/probe_didcomm_issuance_token.py` confirms a newly provisioned token
has positive TTL and is renewable. A source search found no workload
`renew-self` client or renewal agent in the production Rust, Compose and
Kubernetes paths. Renewable at creation therefore is not proof that a
long-running service keeps its KMS authority through expiry. KMS-only release
qualification needs a scoped token lifecycle: renew or rotate before expiry,
propagate the replacement without leaking it, reject wrong-policy/wrong-tenant
tokens, and prove signing and DIDComm authcrypt continue across expiry,
restart and OpenBao failover. Keep this as an availability and custody gate;
do not paper over expiry with a local-key fallback.

OpenBao's [Agent auto-auth documentation](https://openbao.org/docs/agent-and-proxy/autoauth/)
states that it renews acquired tokens and reauthenticates when renewal fails.
Its [token-file method documentation](https://openbao.org/docs/agent-and-proxy/autoauth/methods/token_file/)
explicitly excludes that method from production use; wrapping the current
static token files in a token-file Agent is therefore not the release design.
Use a workload identity authentication method (Kubernetes identity in that
deployment, and a supported non-static-token identity in self-host) with
scoped policies and a protected file sink or local Agent proxy. Verify the
actual service reads replacement credentials or uses the proxy after
reauthentication, including a short-lease expiry and Raft failover probe.

K6 authorization implementation inventory: Flow's verification-start HTTP
handler authorizes the principal for `verification:execute` on the requested
organization and persists the resulting instance before its public request
object route calls the signer. That stored instance and the exact signing
input are suitable authority facts for a purpose-scoped signing grant; the
current `SigningRequest` carries neither its instance ID nor a proof. Native
Issuance reuses `HttpDidSigner` from credential building, Canvas LTI tool
signing, and Canvas readiness. A replacement signer boundary must carry
separately authorized operation context for all three owners, not just Flow
or the credential builder. The direct Gateway compatibility route currently
accepts only the shared issuer credential and a query tenant and should be
removed or gated by the same verified proof. Signing Keys must reject a
valid service credential paired with another tenant or altered payload
before remote KMS invocation.

Further K6 authority-source audit: Flow's HTTP `authorize` reads the
gateway-supplied `x-user-id` and checks organization membership, while Gateway
removes a caller's forged `x-user-id` before forwarding and then inserts its
trusted identity. Request-object signing can occur later on a public wallet
GET, after Flow has persisted the authorized instance; the original user
session is not a signer request credential. Any purpose-scoped grant should
therefore be issued from the authorized start/instance record and bound to
the eventual signing bytes. Signing Keys must verify it independently; merely
forwarding `x-user-id` or trusting Flow's body tenant repeats the current
cross-tenant gap. The exact grant issuer/verifier and replay control remain
an implementation gate.

K6 deferred-sign detail: verification start already stores the authorized
principal as `_marty_verification_principal_id` in the Flow instance context,
alongside the resolved signing identity. A later public wallet GET loads that
instance, prepares the compact JWT, asks the signing provider to sign its
exact JWS input, and only then compare-and-swaps the request snapshot. The
current `SigningRequest` omits instance ID, principal and any authority
proof, and the HTTP provider forwards a caller-selected organization in both
query and body. The stored principal and organization can anchor a delegated
request-object operation, but Signing Keys must verify the grant against an
authority independent of the caller, bind it to the exact JWS input and
issuer profile, and reject replay before remote KMS. The current post-sign
snapshot compare-and-swap cannot serve as the replay guard because two
concurrent GETs can both reach the signer before one loses the swap. Preserve
the public wallet retrieval and authorized start behavior while moving the
authorization and one-use decision ahead of the remote sign.

K6 sibling-route authority audit: the public
`POST /v1/signing-keys/services/{service_id}/sign` route is guarded by a
dedicated Gateway-only static credential. Gateway inserts it only after
`signing-key:create` authorization and replaces caller-supplied tenant query
scope. Direct Signing Keys access with that credential still accepts a
caller-selected tenant and registered service/key reference; the backend
checks binding within the stated tenant but receives no independently
verifiable proof of that tenant authorization or exact originating operation.
The issuer-DID grant design must cover this public service-sign route too,
including direct-backend wrong-tenant and replay tests. A Gateway credential
is transport authentication, not tenant authority. Preserve the authorized
Gateway path and the existing purpose/algorithm/reference checks while
closing this sibling route; do not infer its safety from removal of the old
internal service-sign alias.

K6 tenant-signing grant acceptance matrix for the next cohesive Rust feature:

| Signing origin | Authority fact to preserve | Pre-KMS verification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gateway public service-sign | Authorized principal has `signing-key:create` in the Gateway-selected organization. | Signing Keys verifies a one-use grant for that organization, service, algorithm and exact payload; direct use of the transport key alone fails. |
| Flow wallet request object | Authorized verification start persisted the organization, principal, instance and issuer identity before the later public wallet GET. | Signing Keys verifies a one-use grant bound to that instance and exact JWS input before signing; concurrent GETs cannot both consume it. |
| Issuance credential, Canvas LTI/readiness and passport SOD | Each machine or user entry point has its own authorized tenant and operation record. | Signing Keys verifies the specific origin, tenant, key purpose, algorithm and exact bytes; a generic Issuance service credential cannot select another tenant. |
| Gateway issuer-DID compatibility route | Supported Flow and Issuance consumers use this route; the query tenant and static credential are not independent authority. | Require a verified one-use grant bound to the producer's authorized operation and exact bytes. |
| Signing Keys certificate CSR and managed issuer certificate paths | Gateway-approved service/issuer and certificate ceremony authority, including tenant, operator and key purpose. | Carry an operation-specific authority through internal `sign_with_issuer_did` and the direct service CSR `kms::sign` call before any KMS signature. |

The grant must have an independently trusted issuer, bounded lifetime and
atomic one-use record before KMS invocation. A second shared service key or
HMAC over caller-selected fields alone is not tenant authorization. Negative
acceptance must cover wrong tenant, altered payload/purpose/key reference,
replay, concurrent consumption, expired grant, direct backend bypass and
backend outage. Keep public wallet retrieval and authorized machine flows
working through the new proof rather than reverting to local signing.

K6 Azure signature-format qualification finding: the Signing Keys adapter
currently labels every ECDSA provider response as DER, and its Azure ES256
golden vector supplies a synthetic DER response. Microsoft's [Key Vault
algorithm reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/key-vault/keys/about-keys-details)
and [Sign REST contract](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/rest/api/keyvault/keys/sign/sign?view=rest-keyvault-keys-2025-07-01)
describe ES256/384/512 by RFC 7518; [RFC 7518 section
3.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7518.html#section-3.4) defines a
fixed-width R||S signature. This is evidence that the adapter's DER assumption
may be wrong, but those documents do not explicitly demonstrate the actual
Azure response bytes. Before claiming Azure support, capture a real Key Vault
ES256 response with a non-exportable test key, verify it against the returned
public key, and correct provider-specific encoding and golden vectors as
needed. Also exercise ES384/ES512 if advertised. Do not treat the current
mock DER vector as cloud interoperability evidence.
The certificate and CSR handlers in `signing-keys/src/http.rs` currently
require `signature_encoding == "der"` in three paths. If Azure returns
RFC 7518 R||S, a provider-label correction alone would reject those flows;
the fix must convert the validated signature to DER at the certificate/CSR
boundary while retaining JOSE form for credential signing. Cover both
consumers with provider-real acceptance before changing the advertised
capability.

K6 signing-grant implementation direction: use OpenBao Transit HMAC keys as
non-exportable, separately policy-scoped grant issuers for Gateway, Flow and
Issuance operations. OpenBao's [Transit API](https://openbao.org/docs/next/api/secret/transit/)
supports `/transit/hmac/:name` and `/transit/verify/:name` with versioned HMAC
results. Each producer may call HMAC only after its own authorization check
has resolved an authoritative organization and operation record: Gateway's
`signing-key:create` decision, Flow's persisted verification instance, or
Issuance's authorized credential/passport/Canvas operation. The grant input
must encode a versioned domain, producer identity, operation/record ID,
organization, route/service or issuer DID, key purpose, algorithm, exact
payload digest, issued/expiry times and a random one-use ID. Signing Keys
holds verify-only Transit policy and checks this canonical input against the
parsed signing request, bounded clock, and an atomic Redis one-use consume
before any signing KMS call. Producer service credentials remain transport
authentication, not substitutes for this grant. Separate origin policies
must prevent a Flow token from minting Gateway or Issuance grants. Fail
closed when Transit verification or replay storage is unavailable. Add
wrong-tenant/payload/purpose/key/operation, expiry, replay, concurrent-use,
direct-backend and outage tests; prove live OpenBao policy denial and allowed
wallet/credential paths. This is an implementation design, not completed K6
authority evidence.

K6 grant foundation, local UI batch: added a shared Rust `marty-signing-grant`
crate for versioned, domain-separated canonical claim bytes and exact operation
binding. Claims cover producer, operation ID, tenant, route, service/issuer,
key reference/purpose, algorithm, SHA-256 of the payload, short expiry and a
one-use nonce. The crate rejects malformed, expired, wrong-tenant, wrong-key,
wrong-purpose and altered-payload claims before invoking a KMS verifier; it
contains no secret key or local HMAC implementation. Its focused tests and
warnings-denied Clippy pass. This is contract groundwork only: producers,
OpenBao HMAC/verify, atomic replay, policies and live sign-route enforcement
must be implemented before claiming tenant authorization.

K6 grant Transit client, local UI batch: the shared Rust crate now calls the
mounted OpenBao `hmac` and `verify` endpoints with SHA-256, validates a
versioned 32-byte HMAC, bounds responses, rejects redirects, and returns
sanitized failures without local MAC keys. Its synthetic HTTP tests and
warnings-denied Clippy pass. An opt-in test also passed against a fresh
disposable loopback OpenBao 2 dev instance with a marked KV guard, a
non-exportable Transit key, and distinct 10-minute mint-only and verify-only
tokens. It proved mint/verify, altered-input denial, and cross-policy denial;
the instance was stopped. This proves the proposed KMS primitive and policy
split, not yet the Gateway/Flow/Issuance authorization or one-use sign path.

K6 replay foundation, local UI batch: an OpenBao-verified grant has a private
Rust type that only a successful bound `verify` call can construct. A shared
Redis store consumes that type with one `SET ... NX EX` before issuer KMS
signing, using a short bounded TTL and failing closed on expiry or datastore
failure. The focused concurrent-consumer test passed against fresh marked
disposable loopback Redis DB 13: exactly one caller consumed the grant, and
replay/expiry were denied. The container was stopped. Gateway/Flow/Issuance
routes are not yet wired to this verifier and replay store, so K6 tenant
authority is still open.
Grant API self-review removed caller-supplied clocks from the public
verification and replay-consumption methods. Both now read the process clock
internally, so a route cannot accidentally extend an expired grant by passing
a stale timestamp. The internal fixed-time test path remains private. The
grant suite, warnings-denied Clippy and disposable concurrent Redis test
pass after this change.

K6 origin-policy self-review, local UI follow-up: the production Transit
client now selects one fixed, distinct HMAC key name for each of the six
signing origins, and bound verification rejects a client for another origin
before contacting OpenBao. The arbitrary key-name constructor is private to
the grant crate for isolated tests. This makes the intended separate
mint-policy boundary explicit in Rust; the corresponding OpenBao keys,
policies, service token mounts and sign-route checks are still required.

The grouped UI head `9c91af91f` started [exact-head
CI](https://github.com/ElevenID/marty-ui/actions/runs/38117216842). Its early
Rust feature probe and Rust lint jobs failed because their independent
KMS-only Core revision guard and standalone probe lock still pinned the older
`7f276a4` source while both production Rust roots pin reviewed `6acba9d`.
The local follow-up updates that guard and only the six Core source records in
the probe lock. Both production and standalone `cargo metadata --locked`
checks, including the Core boundary script, pass locally. Hold this correction
with the origin-policy follow-up until the current run is terminal.

K6 OpenBao policy groundwork, local UI follow-up: canonical OpenBao bootstrap
now provisions six distinct, non-exportable HMAC keys with plaintext backup
disabled. It writes one exact `/sha2-256` mint-only policy per signing origin
and one verify-only policy listing only those six exact paths. A fresh
disposable OpenBao 2 dev instance ran the full bootstrap, and scoped tokens
proved Gateway mint and Signing Keys verify, while a Flow mint token could
not mint Gateway grants, the verifier could not mint, the minter could not
verify, and the minter could not read the key. The instance was stopped.
This does not yet provision or mount those tokens in supported deployments,
or enforce grants on production signing routes.

K6 self-host grant-token provisioning, local UI follow-up: the Raft bootstrap
now creates six mint-only no-default-policy orphan tokens and one verify-only
token in distinct runtime files, rejecting reused files with unexpected
policies or identity. The full bootstrap and an idempotent rerun passed on a
fresh disposable OpenBao 2.7.1 Raft instance. All seven files were present;
Gateway mint and Signing Keys verify succeeded, while Flow-to-Gateway mint,
verify-token mint, mint-token verify and mint-token key-read attempts failed.
The disposable container and volumes were removed. Runtime mounts/config,
producer authorization and sign-route enforcement remain open.

The external self-host OpenBao bootstrap now emits the same seven scoped
grant-token files beside its existing service credentials. Its shell syntax
and diff hygiene pass locally; unlike the Raft bootstrap, this external
bootstrap path has not yet had a live end-to-end run. Neither supported
runtime mounts nor grant enforcement is complete.

K6 shared grant wire contract, local UI follow-up: the Rust crate now mints a
single `GrantEnvelope` with canonical claims and a random 122-bit UUID-v4
one-use ID, a 30-second expiry from the process clock, and an OpenBao HMAC.
It rejects a producer client configured for another origin, and exposes a
matching envelope verifier. The synthetic Transit HTTP test exercises mint,
verify and altered-payload rejection; the crate suite and warnings-denied
Clippy pass. Production services still need authoritative operation binding,
scoped token mounts and fail-closed route use before this grants any signing
authority.

The grant envelope also has one bounded URL-safe header encoding for all
producer-to-Signing-Keys paths. It rejects malformed, oversized or multiline
values before JSON parsing; its synthetic mint/header/verify test and
warnings-denied Clippy pass. Gateway still must replace any caller-supplied
grant header, and Signing Keys must bind and consume it before KMS signing.

The `9c91af91f` hosted Rust Contracts job also failed one Gateway managed-key
case: its shared Transit stub returned an ECDSA DER signature for the Ed25519
issuer key. The local fixture now returns a 64-byte Ed25519-shaped response
for that key and retains DER for ECDSA. The exact ignored Gateway-to-Signing-
Keys case passed locally against a fresh marked disposable Redis DB 13 with
the test-only Transit token; that container was stopped. This is a fixture
repair, not live provider cryptographic acceptance. The prior exact-head run
is still active on other jobs; keep the local corrections batched until it
is terminal.

K6 centralized Signing Keys verifier, local UI follow-up: the shared Rust
crate now selects the Transit verifier by trusted route origin, reads its
separate verify-only token file, authenticates and binds the bounded grant
header, then atomically consumes the one-use grant in Redis before returning
authorization. Malformed/mismatched/replayed grants are denied; OpenBao,
token-file or Redis failures are unavailable and stop signing. A fresh
disposable OpenBao 2 dev instance provisioned by the canonical bootstrap,
and a marked disposable Redis DB 13, passed the opt-in concurrent authorization
test: exactly one use succeeded, and a later replay was denied. Both
containers were stopped. This verifier is still not wired into production
routes, so issuer signing is not yet tenant-authorized end to end.

Grant-kernel self-review tightened the authority type: replay consumption
now yields an unforgeable, non-cloneable `ConsumedGrant` instead of `()`.
It retains the authenticated claims and can recheck the exact tenant, route,
operation, key, purpose, algorithm, payload and expiry at the point of KMS
use. This lets the lower signing kernel require proof that cannot be
constructed by a direct backend caller. The crate tests, warnings-denied
Clippy and the fresh disposable OpenBao/Redis concurrent authorization test
pass after the change. Production signing methods have not yet been changed
to require this type.

The kernel call-graph review found that `SigningCompatibilityService` has
both public service and issuer-DID methods, and the latter calls the former.
Signing Keys HTTP also invokes issuer-DID signing from CSR and managed
certificate ceremonies; `generate_public_service_csr` calls `kms::sign`
directly. Those paths must receive operation-specific authority and the
lower-level sign methods must recheck it; guarding only the two HTTP sign
handlers would leave bypasses. Holder/device proof signing is separately
scoped and must retain its supported behavior.

Fresh Issuance schema qualification, local UI evidence: applied all nine
Rust-owned Issuance SQL files (`0000` through `0008`) in order to a new
disposable PostgreSQL 15 container, then ran the canonical
`verify_fresh_kms_issuance_schema.py` catalog check against its exact
container ID. It found no historical Alembic ledger and no private-key
table or column, including `issuer_signing_keys`. The container was stopped.
This proves the Rust Issuance clean-install schema only; assembled supported
stacks and populated-data content scans still need their own evidence.

Gateway grant-header boundary, local UI follow-up: the public proxy now
removes the shared Rust grant header from every caller request before
applying trusted upstream overrides. The signing-mutation regression sends
a forged header and confirms it does not reach Signing Keys while the
authenticated organization and dedicated service-sign credential still do.
That exact Gateway test and warnings-denied library Clippy pass. A trusted
Gateway producer still must mint and insert the header after its authorization
decision; this change alone does not enforce signing grants.

Internal issuer-DID relay, local UI follow-up: Gateway now accepts a bounded,
syntactically valid signing-grant envelope only on its dedicated authenticated
internal issuer-DID signing route and forwards it to Signing Keys as a trusted
upstream header. It continues to override the caller's organization with the
authenticated query scope. The exact relay regression covers malformed-header
rejection, header propagation, and organization override; warnings-denied
Gateway Clippy passes. This is transport plumbing only: Flow and Issuance must
mint appropriately scoped grants, and Signing Keys must authenticate, consume,
and recheck them at every relevant signing kernel entry before K6 is complete.

Signing-kernel call inventory for K6 implementation: issuer signing enters
through public service sign, internal issuer-DID sign, managed certificate/DSC
ceremonies that call `sign_with_issuer_did`, and public service CSR generation
that calls `kms::sign` directly. Separately, `managed_holder_key` and
`vc_api_holder_proof` also call `kms::sign` for holder/device proofs. A blanket
grant requirement on the generic KMS adapter would break those supported
holder flows. Introduce an issuer-signing kernel entry that requires a consumed
grant and exact binding, route every issuer/certificate/CSR call through it,
and keep the independently authorized holder/device signing path distinct.
The grant operation identifier must originate with the authorized operation;
the HMAC-authenticated envelope alone cannot turn an arbitrary HTTP request
identifier into tenant authorization.

Grant-use self-review tightened `ConsumedGrant::authorizes` to consume its
proof. Once the Signing Keys kernel requires this value, one replay-store
consumption can permit at most one invocation of the issuer KMS sign entry;
the same Rust proof cannot be borrowed repeatedly to sign twice. The Redis
one-use key still prevents separate requests from consuming the envelope
again. Production kernel wiring and its end-to-end acceptance remain open.

Grouped UI publication: the prior `9c91af91f` [CI
38117216842](https://github.com/ElevenID/marty-ui/actions/runs/38117216842)
finished with 18 successes, including Canvas, OpenBao DIDComm plugin image
and Rust service images. Rust Feature Regression Probe and Rust Lint failed on
the stale standalone Core revision; Rust Contracts failed on the mismatched
Ed25519 acceptance stub; CI Gate failed downstream. Local corrections passed
their focused checks. UI #1192 head `27c154b39` publishes the 18-commit
correction and grant-foundation batch; its PR body records the incomplete
tenant-authority gate. New exact-head checks are running.

Credentials Core repin: draft PR #313 head `46d5a63` now pins Core
`6acba9d9e079cfba7ae9f94356899b29c93466b0` across all five direct
dependencies, six locked Core packages and its production graph guard.
Locked offline metadata and the graph guard passed; local Rust tests passed
25 library, three isomdl digest and two doc cases, and all-target warnings-
denied Clippy passed. The previous `d562739` head was green; the new head has
19 successful hosted checks and no failures. Release artifact qualification
and protected review remain pending.

Flow signing-origin review, local follow-up: the request-object builder now
passes its validated Flow instance ID into `SigningRequest` as the operation
identifier that a future Flow Transit grant must bind. The request-object
behavior suite confirms both OID4VP and SIOP signs use the exact instance ID.
Initial request-object signing happens during preparation before the instance
is persisted; a later reissue uses a loaded record. Flow grant minting must
therefore rely on the already authorized and validated operation context,
not claim that every signed request has a preexisting database row. The grant
header, token mount and Signing Keys enforcement remain to be wired.

Shared grant minter, local follow-up: `GrantMinter` fixes one origin-specific
Transit key at construction and reads its dedicated token file for each mint,
so token rotation does not require process restart. Mint and verifier use one
bounded token-file reader that rejects missing, oversized, multiline and
non-printable credentials without disclosing them. Grant crate tests (seven
passed, three guarded live tests ignored), warnings-denied Clippy and Rustfmt
pass. Production producer configuration, token mounts and end-to-end kernel
enforcement remain open.

Grant route/origin self-review: the shared authenticated-claim validator now
requires a Gateway service origin to bind the service ID in its exact public
sign route and forbids an issuer DID there. Issuer-DID origins require the
exact internal issuer-DID route, an issuer DID and no service ID. This stops
an origin-scoped Transit mint token from being used for a different signing
route even if a caller could supply matching request fields. Eight local
grant tests and warnings-denied Clippy pass. Certificate and CSR ceremonies
need explicit, separately reviewed route/authority shapes before kernel
enforcement; they cannot silently reuse an unrestricted issuer grant.

Issuance signing-origin call review: `credential_builder::SignRequest` is
shared by four production paths, not only credential materialization.
Credential construction has a reserved credential ID assigned from the
authorized transaction before commit. Passport SOD signing has a persisted
`PassportJob.id` at `PassportHttpService::sign`; Canvas LTI signing is used
for deep-linking, OAuth client assertions and readiness JWTs; Canvas DID
readiness also signs a generated challenge. Adding a required operation ID
at the common signer boundary correctly exposed each caller at compile time,
but there is no honest single default ID for them. The attempted cross-path
field change was reverted before commit. Wire authorized operation IDs through
each producer first, with Canvas launch/session or generated assertion IDs
and the passport job ID, then require the field and mint exact-payload grants.
Do not derive tenant authority merely from an arbitrary payload hash or add a
compatibility default. The HTTP grant header, token mounts and Signing Keys
enforcement remain open.

Flow grant capability self-review: the shared route/origin validator now also
limits `FlowWalletRequest` grants to the actual OID4VP request-object purpose
`oid4vp_request_signing` and ES256. A Flow-scoped mint token can no longer
authenticate a passport/credential key purpose even on the shared issuer-DID
route. The grant suite and warnings-denied Clippy pass locally. Other origin
capability restrictions still require their complete producer call inventories.

Flow grant producer, local grouped follow-up: production Flow now constructs
its fixed `FlowWalletRequest` OpenBao minter from the exact `BAO_ADDR` and an
absolute, dedicated token-file path. Request-object signing decodes the
canonical payload, mints a short-lived grant bound to the validated Flow
instance ID, organization, issuer DID, exact internal route, purpose, ES256
and payload bytes, then sends it in `x-marty-signing-grant`. A missing minter
fails before the signing HTTP request. The development compose stack creates
and mounts a scoped Flow token; self-hosted compose mounts the token generated
by the existing OpenBao bootstrap; Kubernetes requires a separate scoped
operator-supplied token, mounted as a file. The focused Flow HTTP test covers
fail-closed behavior, grant claims and header forwarding; eight request-object
behavior tests, Flow all-target warnings-denied Clippy, shell syntax, YAML
parse and `git diff --check` pass. The published UI PR has not yet received
this local grouped batch.

This is producer wiring only: Signing Keys still accepts the static issuer
sign API key without verifying or consuming the grant. Before any KMS-only
claim, implement exact-request verification, one-use replay consumption and
the origin-specific capability checks in the Rust Signing Keys kernel, then
prove that a missing, changed, expired or replayed grant cannot reach the
remote KMS signing call. Extend the same producer/receiver contract to the
Gateway and the four distinct Issuance signing call paths, with their actual
operation authority. Review and qualify token provisioning and rotation in
each deployment model.

Exact Flow key binding, local grouped follow-up: the Signing Keys issuer
resolver now projects the selected remote `signing_key_reference` beside the
public verification method. Flow requires that reference in its validated
signing identity, carries it into `SigningRequest`, and binds it in the OpenBao
grant and signing request body. The Signing Keys compatibility signer rejects
a supplied reference if the selected issuer profile changed after resolution.
This closes the key-selection gap during a Flow request-object sign without
exporting key material. The shared language-neutral issuer identity vector
was updated. Flow's 44 library and eight request-object tests, Signing Keys'
ten compatibility tests, both crates' all-target warnings-denied Clippy and
`git diff --check` pass locally with one Cargo job. The broad all-test build
initially exhausted local memory with parallel Rust compilers; targeted
single-job checks completed. This is still producer/resolver binding; the
Signing Keys grant verifier and replay gate remain mandatory before the
remote KMS call and before this can be called KMS-only enforcement.

Signing Keys issuer-DID receiver, local grouped follow-up: the Rust route now
requires a syntactically bounded grant header and a requested key reference
even when the static API key is valid. It reconstructs the binding from the
exact body payload, tenant, issuer DID, key reference, purpose and algorithm,
verifies the origin-specific HMAC with a separate OpenBao verify-only token,
atomically consumes the nonce in Redis, and rechecks the consumed proof before
calling the compatibility signer. The shared grant validator forbids
issuer-DID grants without a key reference. Signing Keys production startup
requires the verifier's OpenBao endpoint and absolute token file. Development,
self-hosted and Kubernetes manifests supply a dedicated verifier token mount;
Kubernetes secret setup requires an operator-supplied verify-only token.
Self-review split development Compose into disjoint Flow-mint and
Signing-Keys-verify volumes, so neither runtime mounts the other's token;
the trusted OpenBao bootstrap alone writes both scoped files.
The OpenBao image runs as UID 100 and cannot write a fresh named Docker
volume at these paths; a disposable image/volume probe reproduced the
permission failure. Development `openbao-init` now runs as root only for
bootstrap, writes read-only files, and the separate runtime mounts stay
read-only. The same disposable image/volume probe confirmed the corrected
write and mode.
Static API-key-only requests now fail closed on the issuer-DID HTTP route.
The Signing Keys unit suite passes 184 tests (nine live tests ignored); the
grant crate passes eight tests (three live tests ignored); all-target
warnings-denied Clippy, shell syntax, manifest parsing and diff checks pass.

The public `/v1/signing-keys/services/{id}/sign` route now also rejects a
static API key without a bounded grant and binds a fixed GatewayService
origin, exact service path and ID, tenant, key reference, purpose, algorithm
and decoded payload before the same OpenBao verification and Redis one-use
consumption. A focused HTTP test proves missing or malformed grants fail
before backend access; all-target warnings-denied Clippy passes. The two
routes share one consumed-proof helper. `sign_with_service` can still be
called from other in-process paths, and direct KMS signing calls serve CSR
and holder-proof work. Do not describe this as a kernel-wide gate. Next
thread a move-only consumed proof, or a separately verified ceremony
authority, through each issuer signing call to its exact KMS invocation;
wire the remaining Gateway and Issuance grant producers and add live
HMAC/replay/KMS-denial acceptance. The published UI PR passed all 28 checks;
the current local batch has not yet been pushed.

Gateway public service-sign producer, local grouped follow-up: the Rust
Gateway now discards caller-supplied signing grants and mints a fixed
`GatewayService` OpenBao Transit HMAC grant after authenticated tenant and
`signing-key:create` authorization. Its binding uses the Gateway-issued
operation ID, exact service route and ID, tenant, explicit key reference,
purpose, algorithm, and decoded payload (base64 or hex). Gateway startup
requires an absolute, Gateway-specific mint token file. The development
OpenBao bootstrap creates a separate mint-only Gateway token and volume;
self-hosted Compose and Kubernetes mount only that token into Gateway. The
Signing Keys verifier retains its separate verify-only token. Explicit key
reference, purpose and algorithm are now required on this public sign route
so the caller cannot change an implicit key choice after the grant is minted;
this is an intentional contract tightening in a predeployment product. This
work still does not put a consumed proof at the final signing kernel call.
The remaining issuer-DID producers, in-process signing paths, live
OpenBao/Redis denial evidence, and deployment token qualification remain
open before the KMS-only goal can be declared complete.
The Gateway library suite passed 163 tests with one pre-existing live test
ignored; its all-target warnings-denied Clippy, focused grant-path tests,
deployment YAML and shell parsing, and scoped token-mount checks passed.

Post-publication least-privilege review found that Gateway still received an
unneeded general OpenBao token in development and self-hosted Compose. Gateway

push after the currently running UI CI reaches a terminal result.
The published `578683999` UI CI run exposed an unreviewed self-host Compose

`test_selfhost_native_owner_compose.py` gate now passes for default, empty,

The same `578683999` run's Canvas lane then failed in its resolved Kubernetes
runtime proof. The release-evidence Rust composer intentionally checks the
Signing Keys deployment against an exact approved environment and mount set;

The hosted Release Contract lane also exposed closed consumer fixtures: the

Final-sign inventory for the next authorization batch: `compat::sign_with_service`
reaches `kms::sign` and is used by both public service-sign and DID-mediated
paths; the two HTTP routes currently consume grants *before* calling it, but
the compatibility kernel takes no consumed proof. Five certificate/CSR paths
inside Signing Keys call `sign_with_issuer_did` directly after their own route
authorization; public service CSR calls `kms::sign` directly. Managed holder
proof signing has separate wallet-owned authority and must remain functional.
Introduce a move-only, exact-request issuer authorization at the final sign
entry, with separately typed ceremony authority for the authenticated
certificate/CSR operations. Recheck resolved key reference and actual signing
bytes there; never let a shared static API key or a JSON tenant field mint that
authority. Preserve holder proof through its separately qualified path.

The branch has since merged the current `main` to test the exact review head.
The merged release transaction requires three gate roles, so the self-host
product descriptor now checks the shared `REQUIRED_GATE_ROLES` set rather than

grant-mint file for development and self-hosted Compose. The shared Flow
provider vector includes the required explicit signing key reference and a

the three grant mint/verify roles or reuse of a general OpenBao service token.
The combined focused deployment, descriptor, Flow fixture and secret tests
pass locally (206 tests); the Flow provider contract passes all eight Rust

The grouped correction now reads the scoped verifier token from the disposable

Local final-sign work has begun in the shared Rust signing-grant crate. A
`ConsumedGrant` can now be consumed against a `FinalSignBinding` built from the
resolved tenant, route, service or issuer DID, key reference, purpose,
algorithm, and actual signing bytes. The proof supplies its own authenticated
origin and operation ID, so callers cannot substitute those values at this
last check. Focused service and DID mutation tests pass, as does warnings-denied
all-target Clippy. This is not yet wired into Signing Keys' final KMS call;
the certificate/CSR ceremony authority and direct CSR path remain open. Keep
the work local for the next cohesive authorization batch rather than triggering

Authorization review before wiring the proof found that issuer certificate CSR
and service CSR are separate public Signing Keys routes. The issuer CSR handler
reaches `sign_with_issuer_did` after profile and tenant checks but has no
Signing Keys-side action credential or grant check; the service CSR handler
calls `kms::sign` directly. Gateway supplies trusted tenant scope and checks
its public-route permission, but that context is not a move-only authority at
the provider boundary. The CSCA/DSC issuance routes do check their distinct
Gateway operator credentials and actor identity before their certificate
signs. Do not construct a generic certificate exception from an arbitrary
tenant JSON field or shared service key. The cohesive authorization batch must
give both CSR routes an authenticated scoped producer and carry a typed,
exact-request proof through all five issuer certificate/CSR signs and the
direct service CSR call, alongside the grant proof for service and issuer-DID
signing. Preserve their existing certificate and holder-proof behavior.

The next local signing batch now passes the consumed OpenBao/Redis grant into
the Signing Keys compatibility signer and rechecks its bound tenant, resolved
key, purpose, algorithm and actual payload immediately before `kms::sign`.
The public service and internal issuer-DID routes no longer discard the
consumed proof at HTTP. The five issuer certificate/CSR calls use a separate
move-only, exact-request in-process authority tied to their selected profile;
those ceremonies still need authenticated scoped producer evidence, and public
service CSR still calls `kms::sign` directly. This is progress toward, not
completion of, final KMS authorization. A focused certificate mismatch test
and the full Signing Keys library suite pass (185 active, 9 ignored).

The `5db9a4b7f` hosted Contracts lane failed three Gateway executable smoke

The Signing Keys full-library run also exposed one stale contract assertion:

The service-CSR producer/consumer batch has begun locally in the shared Rust
grant crate. `ServiceCsrIntent` now has one canonical subject/key/algorithm
encoding for Gateway and Signing Keys; its untrusted body tenant is excluded
because the authenticated tenant is bound separately in the grant. The fixed
Gateway service origin can authorize the `/certificate-csr` route only for an
explicit key reference and `x509_csr` purpose. Shared grant tests pass (12
active, three opt-in live tests ignored) and warnings-denied Clippy passes.
Gateway minting, Signing Keys verification, the transition from verified
intent to an exact generated-CSR signing proof, and live KMS acceptance remain
open. Do not publish this partial feature independently.

The shared grant crate now derives a move-only `ApprovedServiceCsrSign` only
after one consumed Gateway service grant matches the canonical CSR intent,
resolved tenant/service/key/algorithm and generated CSR signing bytes. It
rechecks those exact bytes and expiry at the final sign call. Focused CSR
mutation tests and warnings-denied Clippy pass. Gateway and Signing Keys have
not yet adopted this API, so the service CSR route remains unprotected.

The same hosted run's Rust Service Images lane failed at its Gateway image
health smoke: the container exited before Docker exposed port 8000 because
the workflow omitted the new OpenBao grant minter settings. The local CI

and Canvas lanes are still running at this observation.

The current `5db9a4b7f` hosted release-contract lane has now completed

The local service-CSR batch now uses that shared intent and exact-sign proof

The next producer audit found that Issuance's shared `HttpDidSigner` still
sends its DID signing request without a grant. Its credential, Canvas and
passport callers have different legitimate origins, while the resolved
`IssuerContext.raw_context` already contains the profile-selected remote key
reference. Carry that resolved reference and an explicit origin through the
shared Rust `SignRequest`, give each producer its own scoped OpenBao mint
token, and bind tenant, DID, key, purpose, algorithm, route and exact payload
before the Gateway forwards to Signing Keys. Do not infer an origin from
credential format or mint a broad Gateway grant for arbitrary body fields.
The current hosted head remains active; keep this producer work local until
its CI evidence is collected.

Issuance producer design audit: `HttpDidSigner` currently has no grant header,
origin, operation ID or key reference. Credential context parsing validates
`signing_key_reference` in the resolved response but only retains it in
`raw_context`; make it a typed value at the signing boundary so the grant
binds the key selected by the issuer profile. Canvas's resolved identity
returns the full resolver response, but its signature-provider trait passes
only tenant, DID, verification method and bytes. Extend that trait with the
validated resolved key reference and an operation ID supplied by each Canvas
caller. Passport's managed context likewise retains profile, method and
certificate but drops the resolved key reference; pass the persisted job ID
from `PassportHttpService::sign` and the validated reference into the shared
signer. Configure three fixed-origin minters with separate token files for
credential, Canvas and passport operations, and require a grant before any
production signing HTTP call. The existing bootstrap creates their scoped
OpenBao policies, but Issuance has no minter dependency or production token
mount yet. Also narrow each Issuance origin's route/purpose/algorithm
capabilities in the shared grant crate after the final caller inventory;
currently those three origins accept the generic issuer-DID route shape.

Issuance origin capability hardening, local grouped follow-up: the shared
grant validator now limits the credential token to `vc_jwt_issuer` or
`mdoc_dsc`, the Canvas token to `lti_tool_signing` with RS256, and the
passport token to `x509_doc_signer`. This prevents a compromised producer's
scoped OpenBao token from authenticating another Issuance product's purpose
on the shared issuer-DID route. The bound request still requires an exact
tenant, DID, resolved key, algorithm, payload and operation match. The
cross-purpose regression, all signing-grant unit tests (16 pass, three
explicitly live-only ignored) and warnings-denied all-target Clippy pass
locally. This narrows existing claims; producer minting and operation-record
authority remain to implement before K6 is complete.

The shared Rust process fixture now supplies a dead loopback OpenBao endpoint
and a nonexistent absolute token path for all four Issuance origins; the image

authorize no signing. The Rust fixture compiled with toolchain 1.95 and passed
targeted rustfmt; the Python image-fixture suite passed 12 tests. This batch,
including the local distinct-token preflight, remains unpushed until the
active hosted run concludes.

The run concluded with those two fixture failures and one Canvas self-host
acceptance failure. The latter was an obsolete hard-coded count in the
owned-service recovery validator: its mount allowlist already named all ten
current Issuance secrets, including the four grant tokens, but the final
cardinality check still expected six. The validator and synthetic fixture now
share one exact mount list, so allowed names and count cannot drift. The
targeted Rust recovery test passes on toolchain 1.95. All other hosted jobs,
including OpenBao Raft recovery, passed on `38138126662`; its CI Gate failed
as expected from the three failed jobs. The next grouped push combines the
three corrections and the local distinct-token preflight.

The grouped correction head `900568fae` is published as UI PR #1192; its

bundle lock, binds its Issuance runtime and migration roles, runs all four
native schema owners and verification twice, and scans the assembled database
for private-key schema and content. It also rejects reused root, service and
Notification OpenBao tokens without printing them. The scoped and base probe
tests pass 22 cases with one optional live-Docker case skipped; Ruff and diff
checks pass. This merge and follow-up remain local until the active CI run
concludes, to avoid overlapping full CI runs.

On the published `900568fae` head, Release Contract Tests failed only the six

`c98129b90` integration fixes that mismatch and passes its 22 focused tests.
Rust Service Tests (contracts) found one additional stale Kubernetes model
assertion: the legacy Issuance deployment already has the fixed-origin
signing-grant mount, so adding two DIDComm mounts yields three, not two. The
local assertion now retains the grant mount, removes only the two new mounts
when comparing the complete legacy model, and checks the native two-mount
suffix. Its focused test passed on Rust 1.95; 14 of 15 tests in that file
passed locally, with the remaining CLI test requiring a Linux executable.
The image, Canvas and OpenBao lanes were still active at this checkpoint.

Run `38140853256` ended with those Release and Kubernetes contract failures
plus six Canvas composition failures; the OpenBao plugin/Raft recovery,
packaged image, worker, self-host runtime, Flow, feature probe, lint and
CodeQL lanes passed. Canvas native renewal reserved status entries but never
reached issuer signing because the process fixture used a deliberately dead
OpenBao address and absent signing-grant tokens. Inspection also found a
deployment gap: the native Kubernetes Issuance template had no `BAO_ADDR` or
four origin-specific signing-grant token mounts. The local correction adds
those mounts to the closed template and renderer, asserts their presence in
the composed contract, and gives the host-only renewal acceptance process a
disposable, non-exportable Transit HMAC key with a narrow credential-origin
mint token. The test process receives that scoped token and the disposable
OpenBao address; other origins retain closed token paths. The focused
Kubernetes model and paired-configuration tests pass locally. The Canvas
acceptance executable compiles locally; the full Linux composition and
Kubernetes child tests still require the next grouped hosted run. This batch
is local and unpushed at this checkpoint.

Auth's self-host target was plaintext and Kubernetes Auth lacked the explicit
HTTPS Organization target; Trust Profile's deployed Rust config requires a
public Organization CA but self-host, beta, and Kubernetes omitted it. The

in self-host/beta/Kubernetes where applicable, and gives Trust Profile an
HTTPS Organization target plus public CA mount in all three deployments.

provider mount allowlist were updated for these public CA mounts. A full
beta Compose render caught missing synthetic Org/RP/CT signer settings in
its test fixture; those are now included. The focused beta, self-host, and
Kubernetes deployment suites pass together (179 tests); Kubernetes YAML
parses and shows the intended Auth/Trust Profile targets and mounts, and
`git diff --check` passes. These are deployment/configuration checks, not
connected RPC acceptance. Auth's production Event Stream gRPC target still
uses plaintext, while Auth disables plaintext by default in production, so
the production Auth graph cannot yet be claimed runnable or KMS-only. That
edge needs a keyless Event Stream server listener and HTTPS client cutover.

Event Stream keyless TLS implementation is now staged on the grouped UI
branch. The Rust listener accepts only a public certificate, trusted OpenBao
CA, scoped token file, and explicit versioned P-256 signer; it rejects the
retired TLS private-key file and requires the remote identity when deployed
with gRPC enabled. Auth now requires an HTTPS Event Stream target when its
remote workload identity is configured and opens that channel with the
public workload CA. The self-host, beta, and Kubernetes deployments have
explicit Event Stream signer settings and secret mounts; Auth targets Event
Stream over HTTPS in each. The secret catalog, stack requirements, self-host
example inputs, Kubernetes secret installer/config map, beta certificate
preflight, and packaged bundle synthetic inputs were updated together.

2026-10-15 Keycloak custody scope correction: the local image behind the
packaged `quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:25.0` tag reports version 25.0.6. The

documents generated realm signing keys; the [matching source](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/blob/25.0.6/services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/keys/AbstractGeneratedRsaKeyProviderFactory.java)
shows the private-material write. This is direct evidence of a default local
private-key custody path and a strong reason to audit Keycloak's separate
database, but it is not yet an inspection of that database's exact tables or
runtime rows. Do not boot the protected Auth fixture with an unqualified
