2026-10-15 direct Keycloak database audit and extension feasibility: read-only,
count-only queries against the running local self-host and beta PostgreSQL
Keycloak databases each found `COMPONENT_CONFIG` with four `privateKey` rows
and four generated symmetric `secret` rows. The private-key rows belong to
`rsa-generated` and `rsa-enc-generated`, one of each in `master` and `11id`;
the secret rows belong to `aes-generated` and `hmac-generated`. No values were
read or printed. The staged `scripts/sql/keycloak-kms-only-verify.sql` rejects
these rows and any non-`marty-openbao-transit` KeyProvider, and requires that
both realms have a remote provider. It failed as intended on both current
databases with counts 4/4/8 and zero remote realms. This verifier is a
release gate target, not a fix or a migration script.

An [upstream Keycloak issue](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/39933)
explicitly identifies current KeyProvider private/secret material in
`COMPONENT_CONFIG`. An [upstream design discussion](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/discussions/22264)
explains that remote KMS signing needs both a public `KeyProvider` and a
`SignatureProvider`, and flags the master-realm bootstrap trap when replacing
built-in signature providers. A [third-party Securosys HSM provider](https://github.com/securosys-com/keycloak-securosys-hsm-provider)
demonstrates external RS256/ES256 signing in Keycloak, but is bound to its
own HSM/JCE/REST backend; it is not an OpenBao Transit solution. The KMS-only
implementation must use a pinned Java Keycloak extension or a proven bridge,
preconfigure both realms before any signing, disable generated/imported/local
provider fallback, preserve JWT/JWKS rotation and login behavior, then pass
the Keycloak database verifier and connected Auth/Gateway journey. The
Keycloak keys/signature SPIs are internal, so pin and regression-test the
exact Keycloak artifact before upgrading.

2026-10-15 Keycloak 25.0.6 bytecode feasibility check: the local matching
`services.jar`, `server-spi.jar`, `server-spi-private.jar`, and `core.jar` were
inspected with `javap`. `KeyProvider` exposes `getKeysStream`, while
`SignatureProvider` exposes signer/verifier contexts; an external RS256 signer
can publish only a public `KeyWrapper` and route the signer context to OpenBao.
This alone cannot retire the other stored secrets. The built-in
`AbstractGeneratedSecretKeyProvider` decodes the component's `secret` value
into a local `javax.crypto.SecretKey` and publishes it through
`KeyWrapper.setSecretKey`. Keycloak has separate content-encryption and
signature provider SPIs. Therefore the implementation must map **all**
active realm operations before choosing hooks: JWT RSA signing/verification,
RSA encryption/decryption if used, HMAC, AES content encryption, and any
session/token use of those providers. OpenBao Transit remote sign, HMAC,
encrypt and decrypt operations must be matched to the exact Keycloak
algorithms and payload formats; do not expose an exportable fake `SecretKey`
or keep the generated AES/HMAC providers for compatibility. Verify bootstrap
of `master` and `11id` before issuing a token, JWKS/public key rotation,
login/refresh/session flows, and fail-closed behavior when OpenBao is down.
The staged read-only SQL verifier was widened from two hard-coded realms to
every realm while still requiring `master` and `11id`; an extra realm can no
longer evade key-custody checks. It was executed against both running local
self-host and beta Keycloak databases and failed as intended on each with
4 private-key entries, 4 local-secret entries, 8 non-remote providers, and
0 of 2 realms with remote providers. No extension or successful Keycloak
journey is yet present.

2026-10-15 K12 bootstrap and backend feasibility correction: direct `javap`
inspection of the pinned Keycloak 25.0.6 jars shows that both
`RealmManager` (new realm) and `ApplianceBootstrap` (master realm) invoke
`DefaultKeyProviders.createProviders`. That method explicitly adds
`rsa-generated`, `rsa-enc-generated`, `hmac-generated` (HS512), and
`aes-generated`; these are the four providers found in each live database.
Merely installing a remote Java `KeyProvider` under a new ID cannot satisfy
KMS-only, because realm creation still inserts generated-provider components
and their current factories store private/secret material. The factory IDs
used during bootstrap must be replaced or safely overridden from first boot.

The live config confirms `rsa-enc-generated` is `RSA-OAEP`, HMAC is `HS512`,
and signing is RS256 in the product realm. Keycloak 25.0.6 also has a
`CekManagementProvider` SPI (`RsaCekManagementProvider`) and direct
`KeyManager.getActiveHmacKey`/`getActiveAesKey` APIs that return
`SecretKey`. [OpenBao's Transit API](https://openbao.org/docs/next/api/secret/transit/)
supports RS256-compatible `pkcs1v15` signing when explicitly selected, but
its documented decrypt input is a Transit ciphertext, not a raw JOSE
RSA-OAEP encrypted CEK. Treat raw JOSE decrypt and arbitrary-IV/AAD AES
compatibility as unproven backend operations; if active Keycloak flows need
them, implement those private operations in the planned Go OpenBao extension
or choose an OIDC provider with a proved remote interface. Do not wire a
partial RS256-only provider into the protected deployment. First qualify a
source-built Keycloak distribution that never creates private material,
then exercise master/11id login, refresh, JWKS/rotation and optional JWE
paths against the remote backend and run the read-only database gate.

`RestartLoginCookie.encodeAndEncrypt` directly obtains ENC and SIG

`jweDirectVerifyAndDecode`. `DefaultKeycloakSession.keys()` directly

previous suggestion to solve it through that SPI alone was too broad.

value would reopen a local-key/algorithm confusion risk and is not accepted
as KMS-only proof. For this pinned version, pursue a source-built Keycloak
patch that routes the complete cookie JWE AES/HMAC encode/decode operation

Further installed finding (2026-10-17): A local rebuilt candidate bundle with a project-scoped network passed both database migrations, but the organization service rejected its production Redis URL: `InvalidConfiguration("production Redis requires TLS")`. Least-privilege renewal design check: The current renewal stages still use `BAO_ROOT_TOKEN_FILE` and the activation checker an operator token, so no production authority boundary is yet claimed. [OpenBao's token API](https://openbao.org/docs/api/auth/token/) supports a named `auth/token/create/:role_name` path whose role can restrict `allowed_policies`, no-default-policy behavior and orphan status; [OpenBao policy rules](https://openbao.org/docs/concepts/policies/) distinguish that from the root/sudo-sensitive generic token-create path and recommend retiring bootstrap root tokens. Next implementation should configure fixed token roles and a constrained renewal identity at bootstrap, permit only the 21 reviewed signer/JWE policy names, and have Rust/Python renewal use the named role while checking the issued token's exact scope and TTL. The renewal identity must also have only the narrow read/CSR/PKI sign/token lookup rights needed to verify existing version-one keys and stage certificates. Prove forbidden-key, policy-edit, mount-edit and generic token-create denials against a real disposable Raft OpenBao before removing root-token dependence. Parent/child token lifetime and recovery must be tested rather than assumed from the API description.

AppRole SecretID rotation (2026-10-19 UTC): Local-only feature commit `08551ec5b` adds a staged `rotate` mode and a `retire` mode for interrupted old-ID revocation. The same scoped operator policy can mint and destroy SecretIDs only for its own fixed AppRole. Rotation authenticates the current identity, mints a replacement, verifies the replacement login and forbidden-operation denials, writes it into a separate private generation, revokes the old SecretID, and checks that old login is rejected. Before replacement files are complete, failure destroys the new remote SecretID and removes local partial files; if revocation fails afterward, the valid new generation remains available for an explicit `retire` retry. The isolated Raft/OpenBao policy was updated to the new source ACL only in the disposable test state. Two real sequential rotations succeeded, the previous credential was denied, the first replacement logged in, and the generated identity files were mode 0600. The `retire` command also succeeded idempotently against an already revoked ID. Focused Linux tests passed 28 with one unrelated skip; Windows tests passed two with four POSIX skips; Ruff and diff checks passed. The isolated OpenBao was stopped, its test toolbox disconnected, and the production site still returned HTTP 200. This closes routine SecretID rotation but not lost-identity recovery, coordinated Raft restore, root-token retirement, CA rollover, or credential-expiry acceptance.
